requirements: Reproduce MultiKernelBench: a multi-platform benchmark for LLM-based DL kernel generation across Nvidia GPUs (CUDA), Huawei NPUs (AscendC), and Google TPUs (Pallas), with 285 tasks in 14 categories, evaluation metrics, and experimental findings.

sub_tasks.requirements: Set up the three hardware platforms (Nvidia L20 GPU, Huawei Ascend 910B2, Google TPU v2-8) with the necessary toolchains (CUDA, AscendC, Pallas/JAX) and PyTorch integration required to run the benchmark.
Provision the three target hardware platforms with the specifications reported in Table 2.
Code has been implemented to detect and confirm that experiments run on a Nvidia L20 GPU (Ada Lovelace) with 48 GB HBM available.
Code has been implemented to detect and confirm that experiments can run on a Huawei Ascend 910B2 NPU (Da Vinci architecture) with 64 GB HBM available.
Code has been implemented to detect and confirm that experiments can run on a Google TPU v2-8 (64 GB HBM) via Google Cloud infrastructure.
The reported FP16 TFLOPS specifications for L20 (59.35), Ascend 910B2 (400), and TPU v2-8 (180) match the values in Table 2 (used for baseline hardware documentation).
Install and configure the CUDA toolchain and PyTorch cpp_extension integration for the Nvidia L20 backend.
Code has been implemented to install a CUDA toolkit (with nvcc) compatible with the L20 GPU and to expose it to PyTorch's cpp_extension utility for JIT compilation.
PyTorch has been installed with CUDA support such that torch.cuda.is_available() returns True and torch.cuda.Event synchronization markers can be used for kernel timing.
Code has been implemented to enable device-side assertions (TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA / CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING) when compiling CUDA kernels, as required for failure analysis.
Install and configure the AscendC toolchain (CANN) and torch_npu integration for the Huawei Ascend 910B2 backend.
Code has been implemented to install the Huawei CANN toolkit including the AscendC compiler and its dependencies required to build custom AscendC kernels.
torch_npu has been installed and configured such that PyTorch can allocate tensors on the Ascend NPU device and torch_npu synchronization APIs are usable for kernel timing.

Glue scripts have been implemented that assemble the AscendC output components (host code, tiling configuration, device code, PyTorch module) into the file structure required by the AscendC compilation pipeline.
Install and configure the JAX/Pallas toolchain and PyTorch bridge for the Google TPU v2-8 backend.
JAX with TPU support has been installed such that jax.devices() reports the TPU v2-8 cores and pallas_call can be imported and executed.

Code has been implemented to bridge JAX-compiled Pallas kernels into PyTorch-compatible modules (converting torch tensors to jax arrays and back) so Pallas kernels can be evaluated against reference PyTorch modules.
Code has been implemented to measure Pallas kernel execution time using JAX debugging/profiling tools (given that Pallas lacks synchronization markers analogous to CUDA/AscendC events).
Ensure a consistent PyTorch eager-mode baseline environment across all three platforms.

Code has been implemented so that reference PyTorch modules always execute in eager mode, with TorchDynamo and other compilation modes explicitly disabled to avoid platform-dependent measurement inconsistencies.

A cross-platform environment specification (e.g., requirements.txt / conda env / docker files) has been provided that pins compatible versions of PyTorch, JAX, torch_npu, and CANN for reproducing the benchmark.

Implement the modular backend abstraction layer that decouples platform-specific logic (device init, compile, execute, verify, cleanup) from the core evaluation pipeline and supports registration of new backends.
The unified Backend interface exists and defines all responsibilities required to abstract platform-specific logic from the core pipeline.
Code has been implemented that defines an abstract `Backend` base class (or equivalent interface) that concrete platform backends must subclass.
Code has been implemented such that the `Backend` interface declares an abstract method for device initialization and hardware identification.
Code has been implemented such that the `Backend` interface declares abstract methods for kernel code compilation and for executing the compiled kernel.

Code has been implemented such that the `Backend` interface declares abstract methods for correctness verification (randomized testing against a reference module) and performance measurement (timing kernel execution).
Code has been implemented such that the `Backend` interface declares an abstract method for resource cleanup and memory management following kernel evaluation.
Instantiating the abstract `Backend` class directly (without subclassing) raises an error, ensuring subclasses must override all required methods.
A backend registration and dynamic loading mechanism enables adding new platforms without changing core evaluation logic.
Code has been implemented that provides a `@register_backend(<platform>)` decorator which registers a backend subclass under a string platform name in a global registry.
Applying `@register_backend('cuda')` (or similar) to a subclass makes that subclass retrievable from the registry keyed by the given platform name.

Code has been implemented that dynamically loads the appropriate backend at runtime given a platform name string (e.g., a `get_backend(name)` factory), instantiating the registered subclass without core-pipeline modifications.
Requesting a backend for an unregistered platform name raises a clear error (e.g., KeyError or a custom exception) rather than silently failing.
Concrete backend subclasses are provided for the three supported platforms (CUDA, AscendC, Pallas), each registered under the unified interface.
Code has been implemented for a CUDA backend subclass registered as `cuda` that implements all abstract methods of the `Backend` interface (init, compile, execute, verify, cleanup).
Code has been implemented for an AscendC backend subclass registered as `ascendc` that implements all abstract methods of the `Backend` interface for the Huawei NPU platform.
Code has been implemented for a Pallas backend subclass registered as `pallas` that implements all abstract methods of the `Backend` interface for the Google TPU platform.
The core evaluation pipeline interacts with backends only through the unified interface, ensuring platform-specific logic is decoupled.

The core evaluation driver code contains no direct platform-specific branching (e.g., no `if platform == 'cuda'` conditionals scattered through the pipeline); it dispatches through the loaded `Backend` instance's methods.

A new backend can be added by implementing a subclass of `Backend` and applying `@register_backend(...)` in a standalone module, without modifying any file in the core evaluation pipeline; adding a stub backend and dispatching to it via the platform-name argument succeeds without touching core code.
An example Triton (or equivalently minimal) backend can be added in fewer than 20 lines of additional code beyond boilerplate, matching the paper's extensibility claim in Section 5.
Construct the 285-task dataset across 14 functional categories, including reference PyTorch modules, input tensors, and the newly added categories (Broadcast, Resize, Optimizer, expanded Indexing).
Dataset totals and category schema match Table 1.

The dataset defines exactly 14 functional categories: Activation, Broadcast, Convolution, Full Architecture, Fusion, Loss, Math, Matrix Multiply, Normalization, Optimizer, Pooling, Index, Resize, and Reduce.
Code has been implemented that exposes each category with a machine-readable identifier so downstream evaluation code can iterate categories and count their tasks.
Per-category task counts match Table 1 exactly.
The Activation category contains exactly 15 kernel tasks.
The Broadcast category contains exactly 10 kernel tasks.
The Convolution category contains exactly 34 kernel tasks.
The Full Architecture category contains exactly 50 kernel tasks.
The Fusion category contains exactly 100 kernel tasks.
The Loss category contains exactly 7 kernel tasks.
The Math category contains exactly 6 kernel tasks.
The Matrix Multiply category contains exactly 17 kernel tasks.
The Normalization category contains exactly 8 kernel tasks.
The Optimizer category contains exactly 5 kernel tasks (newly added category, including tasks such as adam_update and sgd_momentum).
The Pooling category contains exactly 6 kernel tasks.
The Index category contains exactly 12 kernel tasks (expanded from the original 2 tasks in KernelBench, including tasks such as gather and scatter_update).
The Resize category contains exactly 10 kernel tasks (newly added category, including tasks such as bilinear_resize).
The Reduce category contains exactly 5 kernel tasks.
Each task is defined as a reference PyTorch module with input tensors.

Code has been implemented so that every one of the 285 tasks provides a reference PyTorch module (nn.Module subclass) whose forward method invokes official PyTorch operators implementing the reference behavior.

Code has been implemented so that every task provides input tensor specifications (e.g., via a get_inputs function returning concrete tensors such as torch.randn(16, 16384)) usable to drive both the reference and generated modules.
Code has been implemented so that each task additionally exposes any initialization arguments (e.g., a get_init_inputs function) needed to instantiate the reference module deterministically.

For every task in the dataset, instantiating the reference PyTorch module with its declared init inputs and running its forward on the declared input tensors executes without error on CPU/GPU and returns a tensor (or tuple of tensors).
Representative tasks named in Table 1 are present in the dataset.
The Activation category includes representative tasks implementing relu and gelu.
The Broadcast category includes a representative bias_add task.
The Optimizer category includes representative adam_update and sgd_momentum tasks whose reference modules perform the corresponding optimizer state updates.
The Resize category includes a representative bilinear_resize task whose reference module performs bilinear resizing.
The Index category includes representative gather and scatter_update tasks (beyond the original two tasks in KernelBench), reflecting the expansion described in Section 3.3.
The Full Architecture category includes a resnet18 task, and the Fusion category includes a fused_matmul_bias task, matching Table 1's representative tasks.
The dataset is derived from and extends KernelBench tasks as described in Section 3.3.

Code/documentation is in place indicating which tasks originate from KernelBench's original 250 tasks and which are newly added, so the 35-task expansion (285 - 250) is traceable to the Broadcast, Resize, Optimizer, and expanded Indexing categories.

Newly added tasks (for Broadcast, Resize, Optimizer, and the expanded Index category) are sourced from existing kernel libraries such as the PyTorch ATen CUDA native codebase, and each such task's reference implementation matches the semantics of the corresponding library operator.

Categories with few representative tasks or limited relevance (e.g., comparison-related kernels) are excluded from the final 14-category taxonomy, consistent with the pruning step described in Section 3.3.
The dataset is loadable and iterable by the evaluation pipeline in a platform-agnostic manner.

Code has been implemented that provides a dataset loader/API returning the list of tasks (with category label, reference module, init inputs, and input tensor factory) usable by the CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas backends without any platform-specific modifications.
The dataset loader supports filtering tasks by category (e.g., to select all Activation tasks) to enable category-wise evaluation as required by RQ2 and RQ3.

Implement the unified prompt template for the three platforms including system role, one-shot example (default: add), target task, and platform-specific output format specifications for CUDA, Pallas, and AscendC.

The unified prompt template has been implemented with a two-part structure: (1) a platform-specific instruction containing system role, task description, and one-shot example, and (2) the target kernel task consisting of the reference PyTorch module and input tensors.

Code has been implemented that constructs the platform-specific system role string of the form 'You are an expert in writing {platform} kernels ...' where {platform} is substituted with the target platform name (CUDA, AscendC, or Pallas).

Code has been implemented so that the second part of the prompt (kernel task: reference PyTorch module source plus input tensor spec) is generated identically across all three platforms and appended after the platform-specific instruction.

The prompt assembly function returns the final prompt in the order: system role -> output format description -> one-shot example (task + expected output) -> target reference PyTorch module -> target input tensors.

The default one-shot exemplar uses the `add` (vector addition) task across all three platforms, with each platform providing its own reference implementation of add matching the platform's expected output format.

Code has been implemented that stores/loads a CUDA one-shot example for the add task, formatted as self-contained Python code with C++ kernel embedded as a Python string and a PyTorch module invoking the kernel via cpp_extension.

Code has been implemented that stores/loads a Pallas one-shot example for the add task defining a kernel function wrapped with pallas_call along with JAX and PyTorch integration code exposing it as a PyTorch-compatible module.

Code has been implemented that stores/loads an AscendC one-shot example for the add task, containing structured components: host code, tiling configuration, device code, and the PyTorch module wrapper.

The prompt loader can select the one-shot example by (platform, category) pair, defaulting to the add example when no category-specific example is registered, so RQ1/RQ2 use add and RQ3 can swap in category-aware examples without altering other prompt parts.
Platform-specific output format specifications are encoded in the prompt so that generated kernels can be compiled by the corresponding backend pipeline.

The CUDA output format description in the prompt instructs the LLM to emit a single self-contained Python file where CUDA C++ source is embedded as a Python string, loaded via torch.utils.cpp_extension, and exposed through a PyTorch module class whose forward invokes the compiled kernel.

The Pallas output format description in the prompt instructs the LLM to emit self-contained Python code defining a pallas kernel function wrapped by pl.pallas_call with an explicit out_shape via jax.ShapeDtypeStruct, plus JAX<->PyTorch bridging so the result is a PyTorch nn.Module.

The AscendC output format description in the prompt instructs the LLM to emit multiple named components (host code, tiling configuration, device code, and PyTorch module) with clear delimiters/section headers that the AscendC glue script can parse into the required file structure.

Code has been implemented that parses the LLM output for each platform, extracting the code (or the multi-component sections for AscendC) according to the format described in the prompt; parsing succeeds on the corresponding one-shot example verbatim.
The prompt assembly is integrated end-to-end and produces deterministic output that can be reproduced across runs and consumed by all seven evaluated LLMs.

Given a fixed (platform, task, one-shot example) triple, the prompt builder produces byte-identical output on repeated invocation (no nondeterministic ordering of sections, no timestamps, no random IDs).

The reference PyTorch module and input tensor generator (e.g., torch.randn(16, 16384)) inlined into the target-task portion of the prompt come directly from the task definition file, with no manual paraphrasing, so all 285 tasks yield prompts through the same code path.

Implement the platform-specific compilation pipelines that convert LLM-generated text outputs into executable PyTorch modules for CUDA (via cpp_extension), Pallas (via exec of self-contained Python), and AscendC (via glue scripts organizing host/tiling/device components), as described in Sections 3.2 and 3.4.

Implement the shared build pipeline entry point that dispatches LLM-generated text to the appropriate platform-specific compilation logic (CUDA, Pallas, or AscendC) and returns an executable PyTorch module.
Code has been implemented that extracts the code payload from raw LLM text output (e.g., stripping markdown code fences and preamble) before compilation.
Code has been implemented that routes the extracted code to the correct backend compilation function based on the target platform identifier (cuda/ascendc/pallas).
The build pipeline catches compilation exceptions and reports them as compilation failures used by the Compilation@k metric, without crashing the outer evaluation loop.
Implement the CUDA compilation pipeline that turns self-contained Python code (with embedded C++/CUDA source strings) into an executable PyTorch module through torch.utils.cpp_extension.
Code has been implemented that dynamically executes the extracted CUDA-target Python code using exec() in a controlled namespace that exposes torch and cpp_extension utilities.
Code has been implemented that retrieves the resulting custom PyTorch module (e.g., a `ModelNew` class) from the exec namespace and instantiates it for evaluation.
The CUDA pipeline enables device-side assertions during compilation (e.g., via TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA or equivalent flags) to support failure analysis as described in Section 3.4.
The CUDA pipeline invokes nvcc via cpp_extension's JIT loader (load_inline or load) to compile embedded C++/CUDA source into a Python-callable extension.

Given a canonical CUDA add-kernel sample (matching the one-shot example format), the CUDA pipeline compiles it end-to-end and returns a PyTorch module whose forward matches torch.add on random inputs within atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2.
Implement the Pallas compilation pipeline that dynamically executes self-contained Python code containing a pallas_call kernel plus JAX/PyTorch integration glue.
Code has been implemented that runs exec() on the extracted Pallas Python code in a namespace exposing jax, jax.numpy, and jax.experimental.pallas.
Code has been implemented that recovers the resulting PyTorch-compatible module (wrapping a jax.jit'ed pallas_call) from the exec namespace and instantiates it for correctness/performance testing.
The Pallas pipeline handles JAX<->PyTorch tensor conversion (e.g., via dlpack or numpy) so that a torch input tensor can be passed into the compiled pallas_call and a torch tensor is returned.
Given the canonical Pallas add-kernel sample from Figure 1b, the Pallas pipeline executes and returns a PyTorch module whose forward matches torch.add on random inputs within atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2.

Implement the AscendC compilation pipeline, which requires glue scripts to organize multiple LLM-emitted components (host code, tiling configuration, device code, PyTorch module) into the AscendC build layout and produce an executable PyTorch module.

Code has been implemented that parses the LLM output into its four AscendC components (host code, tiling configuration, device code, PyTorch module wrapper) using the delimiters defined by the prompt output format.

Code has been implemented that writes each parsed component into the file/directory layout required by the AscendC toolchain (op host, op kernel, tiling, and Python binding files) inside a per-task build directory.

Code has been implemented that invokes the AscendC compilation toolchain (e.g., custom op build script / msopgen or CMake-based build) as a subprocess and captures stdout/stderr for failure diagnosis.

Code has been implemented that, after a successful AscendC build, loads the produced shared object into Python and exposes it through the LLM-generated PyTorch module wrapper as an executable nn.Module.

The AscendC pipeline detects and reports compilation errors, and specifically preserves the error text (including messages such as 'no member named ...') so that the failure-mode analysis for AscendC (74.8% 'no member named' keyword) can be reproduced.

Given the canonical AscendC add-kernel sample from Figure 1c, the AscendC pipeline builds and loads a PyTorch module whose forward matches torch.add on random inputs within atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2 on Ascend 910B2 hardware.
Ensure the compilation pipelines integrate cleanly with the rest of the benchmark harness (backend abstraction, evaluation, resource management).

Each compilation pipeline is exposed through the unified Backend interface's compile/build method so it can be selected via the @register_backend(<platform>) mechanism without modifying core evaluation code.

Code has been implemented that cleans up per-task build artifacts (temporary directories, loaded extensions) after evaluation to avoid interference between tasks and to support the resource-cleanup responsibility of the backend interface.

Each pipeline returns a structured result that distinguishes between (a) compilation failure, (b) successful compilation, and (c) an instantiated PyTorch module ready for correctness and performance measurement.
Implement the Compilation@k, Pass@k, and SpeedUp_alpha@k metrics along with the randomized correctness testing (N=5, atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2) and platform-specific timing methods.
Compilation@k metric: detect compilation success/failure via exceptions in the platform-specific build pipeline and aggregate across k samples.

Code has been implemented that determines compilation success for a single generated sample by catching exceptions raised during the platform-specific build process (CUDA, AscendC, or Pallas) and returning a boolean success flag with the captured error message.

Code has been implemented that computes Compilation@k as the fraction of tasks for which at least one of the k generated samples compiles successfully, supporting both k=1 (greedy) and k=5 (sampling) settings.

Compilation failure categorization code exists that classifies build errors by keyword matching (e.g., detecting 'no member named' for AscendC API-hallucination errors) to enable failure-mode analysis.
Pass@k metric with randomized correctness testing using N=5 random inputs and tolerance-based comparison.

Code has been implemented that generates N=5 random input tensors matching the reference module's input specification and feeds identical inputs to both the LLM-generated module and the reference PyTorch module.
Code implements the tolerance-based correctness check |output_llm - output_ref| < atol + rtol * |output_ref| with atol=1e-2 and rtol=1e-2 as hard-coded (or configurable) defaults matching the paper.
A single generated sample is considered functionally correct only if all N=5 randomized tests satisfy the tolerance condition; otherwise the sample is marked failed with a diagnostic reason.

Correctness failure diagnostics distinguish at minimum: output value mismatch, output shape mismatch, and runtime exceptions (e.g., CUDA runtime errors, Pallas 'Unexpected Keyword Argument'), and log them for aggregation.
Code has been implemented that aggregates per-sample correctness into Pass@k, reporting the fraction of tasks with at least one correct sample among k samples, for k=1 and k=5.

The correctness pipeline handles reduced-precision reference outputs (e.g., BF16, FP8) without erroring, relying on the atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2 tolerance to absorb precision differences as described in Section 3.5.
SpeedUp_alpha@k metric and platform-specific timing methods for CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas.
CUDA timing code uses torch.cuda.Event synchronization markers placed before and after kernel execution to measure elapsed time between the two events.
AscendC timing code uses torch_npu synchronization markers (analogous to CUDA events) placed before and after kernel execution to compute elapsed time.
Pallas timing code uses JAX/TPU debugging or profiling tools to measure kernel execution time, since synchronization markers are not available in the current Pallas interface.
Reference baseline timings are measured with PyTorch eager mode only, explicitly excluding TorchDynamo and other compilation modes to ensure consistent, reproducible measurements across platforms.
Timing routines include warm-up iterations and repeated measurements to control variance, and the implementation has been validated to yield stable timings across repeated runs on the same machine.

Code has been implemented that computes per-sample speedup as (baseline_time / generated_kernel_time) using the platform-appropriate timing method, only for samples that already passed the correctness check.

SpeedUp_alpha@k is implemented as the fraction of tasks where at least one of k samples is correct AND achieves speedup >= alpha over the PyTorch eager baseline; the implementation supports arbitrary alpha with alpha=1 as the default reported (SU1@k).
Sampling configuration and end-to-end metric reporting harness.

For k=1 evaluation, the harness invokes the LLM with greedy decoding (temperature=0.0); for k=5 evaluation on non-reasoning models it uses stochastic sampling with temperature=0.2 and top_p=0.95, while reasoning models are evaluated only at k=1.

Code has been implemented that reports, per model and per platform, the triple (Comp@k, Pass@k, SU1@k) for both k=1 and k=5, plus a Total Pass count summed across CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas, matching the schema of Table 4.
The metric pipeline supports category-wise breakdowns: it can compute Comp@1, Pass@1, and SU1@1 restricted to tasks within each of the 14 functional categories to reproduce Tables 5-7.

Set up the seven evaluated LLMs (DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen3-235B, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4, DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B-think) with correct decoding parameters (greedy for k=1, temperature=0.2/top-p=0.95 for k=5, no sampling for reasoning models).
Model registry and access configuration for all seven LLMs.

Code has been implemented to register all seven models — DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen3-235B (non-thinking), Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4, DeepSeek-R1-0528, and Qwen3-235B (thinking mode) — with the exact model identifiers/snapshots listed in Table 3.

Code has been implemented to configure API endpoints and authentication credentials for each provider (DeepSeek, Qwen/Alibaba, OpenAI GPT-4o, Anthropic Claude) so that model inference calls can be dispatched from the benchmark driver.

Code has been implemented to tag each model in the registry as either 'non-reasoning' (DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen3-235B, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4) or 'reasoning' (DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B-think), so the driver can select decoding behavior accordingly.
Decoding parameter configuration for k=1 and k=5 evaluations.
Code has been implemented so that for k=1 evaluation on non-reasoning models the sampling parameters are set to greedy decoding with temperature=0.0.
Code has been implemented so that for k=5 evaluation on non-reasoning models the sampling parameters are set to temperature=0.2 and top_p=0.95, and exactly 5 samples are generated per task.

Code has been implemented so that for the two reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-0528 and Qwen3-235B-think) stochastic sampling is disabled: only k=1 (single-generation) evaluation is performed and Pass@5/Comp@5/SU@5 for these models are not obtained via multi-sample decoding.

Code has been implemented to enable Qwen3-235B's thinking mode as a distinct configuration from Qwen3-235B non-thinking (e.g., via the appropriate enable_thinking / think-mode flag), so the same underlying 235B model is invoked in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes.
Generation driver behavior and reproducibility.

Code has been implemented so that the generation driver dispatches the unified prompt template to each configured model and stores each generated sample (5 for k=5 non-reasoning models, 1 for k=1 and reasoning models) with metadata identifying the model, platform, task, and sample index.

Code has been implemented to set a sufficiently large max_tokens / max output length for kernel generation such that outputs are not truncated for long AscendC multi-component outputs, and to retry / handle transient API errors gracefully.

Code has been implemented so that for k=5 sampling runs different random seeds / independent API calls are used per sample to obtain 5 distinct generations, and for greedy k=1 runs the produced sample is deterministic given the prompt.
Reproduce Table 4 results showing overall LLM performance across CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas using the add task as the one-shot example, for both greedy (N=1) and sampling (N=5) settings.

The default-setting experiment runner is implemented and orchestrates end-to-end evaluation of all seven LLMs on all 285 tasks across CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas using the add task as the one-shot example.

Code has been implemented to launch generation runs for each (model, platform) pair over all 285 kernel tasks, iterating over the seven LLMs (DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen3-235B, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4, DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B(think)) and three platforms (CUDA, AscendC, Pallas).
Code has been implemented so that under the default setting the one-shot example provided in the prompt is the add task for every target task, regardless of the target task's category.

Code has been implemented to run each task through both greedy decoding (N=1) and sampling (N=5) modes and persist raw generations along with per-sample metadata (model, platform, task id, seed, decoding mode).

Code has been implemented to skip stochastic N=5 sampling for reasoning-augmented models (DeepSeek-R1-0528 and Qwen3-235B(think)) in the default setting, matching the paper's decision to omit sampling for reasoning models due to inference cost.
Decoding hyperparameters for greedy and sampling runs are configured exactly as described in the paper.
Code has been implemented so that greedy decoding uses temperature=0.0 and produces exactly one sample per task for the N=1 evaluation.
Code has been implemented so that stochastic sampling uses temperature=0.2, top_p=0.95, and generates exactly 5 samples per task for the N=5 evaluation.

Code has been implemented to record per-task generation outcomes (compilation success, correctness pass/fail, measured runtime) for every generated sample, forming the raw evidence for computing @1 and @5 metrics.
Per-platform, per-model aggregation of Comp@k, Pass@k, and SU_1@k is implemented for k in {1,5} and produces the numbers reported in Table 4.
Code has been implemented to compute Compilation@1, Pass@1, and SpeedUp_1@1 for each (model, platform) pair as percentages over all 285 tasks under greedy decoding.

Code has been implemented to compute Compilation@5, Pass@5, and SpeedUp_1@5 for each (model, platform) pair as the fraction of tasks with at least one qualifying sample among the 5 stochastic samples.
Code has been implemented to compute the Total Pass (#) count across all three platforms for each model under both greedy and sampling settings, matching the final Table 4 column.

Code has been implemented to render a Table 4-style summary (rows=models, columns=platform metrics + Total Pass) for both N=1 and N=5 settings, with cells expressed as percentages (except Total Pass which is an integer count).
